In summary, previous studies concerning the corrosion resistance of
LDSs have primarily concentrated on enhancing oxide film density and
stability through compositional optimization via alloying elements. On
the other hand, microalloying increases the smelting cost and promotes
the precipitate formation, thus posing a challenge to the uniformity of
the structure. Consequently, an alternative strategy involving composi
tion preservation coupled with microstructure optimization through
heat treatment has emerged as a promising approach for corrosion
resistance improvement. In recent years, some research has focused on
the critical role of grain size in the corrosion process. Kim et al. [26]
investigated the initial oxidation behavior of austenitic stainless steel
and observed the formation of a double-layer oxide structure near grain
boundaries, whereas nonprotective oxides predominantly formed within
the interior of the grains. Grain refinement was shown to suppress the
formation of rapidly growing spinel oxides, thereby enhancing oxidation
resistance. Nnoka et al. [27] reported that grain refinement increased
passivation coverage by approximately 40 %, with protective oxide
layers preferentially forming along grain boundaries. Mohamed et al.
[28] observed thicker oxide films at high-angle random GBs than at
adjacent grains. This suggests greater anodic activity at the grain
boundaries, which facilitates denser oxide formation. Li et al. [29]
further demonstrated that an increased fraction of special grain
boundaries in weathering bridge steel significantly improved corrosion
resistance. Additionally, Shi et al. [30] found that during the initial stage
of oxidation, GBs with relatively lower potentials typically act as anodic
regions and undergo dissolution. An appropriate GB density helped
homogenize the anodic oxidation current density and made the film
growth more uniform.

Although these studies have established the influence of grain size on
oxide film characteristics in alloys such as stainless steel, they have
mainly focused on the electrochemical behavior or film thickness vari
ations within conventional alloy systems. In the Fe-Mn-Al-C LDSs sys
tem, numerous studies[23,31–33] have investigated the corrosion
behavior of alloys with comparable compositions after similar heat
treatment (solution+aging). These studies predominantly attribute
variations in corrosion resistance to precipitate characteristics. For
example. the formation of precipitates such as carbides not only depletes
the Al element in the matrix, but also intensifies the microgalvanic
coupling between phases. This phenomenon promotes the formation of
corrosion nucleation sites and accelerates the corrosion process.
Furthermore, the segregation of precipitates at GBs induces preferential
corrosion of GBs, which reduces the overall corrosion resistance. In
addition, some studies[22] pointed out that κ-carbide and D0 pre
cipitates frequently serve as the initiation sites for corrosion, reducing
the pitting resistance of LDSs. The distribution and morphology of the
precipitates significantly influence corrosion resistance. However, a
comparison of these references[23,31–33] reveals that the reported
grain sizes differ significantly (9.6 μm-50.2 μm), and the corresponding
pitting potentials also vary considerably (-215 mV~-480 mV) under
similar heat treatment conditions. This phenomenon remains inade-
quately explained in current literature. Similar phenomena were also
found in other LDS investigations[1,22,34,35]. Therefore, in addition to
the effect of precipitates, the grain size evolution during solution
treatment may constitute a critical factor governing the corrosion
resistance of LDSs.
Therefore, in this study, the interference of precipitates was elimi
nated and Fe-Mn-Al-C LDSs with a gradient distribution of grain sizes
(8.7–32 μm) were prepared via solution treatment, and the effects of the
grain size and GB density on evolution of the Al-enrich oxide film were
investigated. The microstructural characteristics of samples with vary
ing grain sizes were systematically characterized by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) tech
niques. The corrosion resistance of the LDSs was comprehensively
assessed through electrochemical testing and immersion experiments.
Furthermore, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Auger elec
tron spectroscopy (AES) were employed to analyze the composition and
structure of the oxide film. Finally, this study reveals the effect of grain
size on the compositional distribution and formation behavior of Al-rich
oxide films on LDSs. We found that grain refinement increased the Al
content in the oxide film and improved the film uniformity. This dis
covery not only enriches the understanding of the surface oxidation
behavior of LDSs, but also provides new ideas and theoretical support for
improving the corrosion resistance of materials through microstructure
regulation.

C) were prepared via a vacuum melting furnace. The steel ingot was

the diffraction patterns are shown in Fig. 1. The diffraction peaks reveal

results indicate that the solution treatment preserves the austenitic
matrix while modifying the relative peak intensities. Notably, the (111)
peak intensity significantly increases following solution treatment,
whereas the (220) peak intensity correspondingly decreases.

4.3. Effects of grain size on oxide film formation and corrosion resistance
of the LDSs
The corrosion resistance of the LDSs exhibits a progressive decline
with increasing grain size and decreasing GB density, with the S950
sample displaying superior corrosion resistance. This variation in
corrosion resistance stems principally from the characteristics of the
oxide film on the LDSs, which are predominantly governed by the
chemical composition and microstructure of the steel[85–87]. Never
theless, experimental evidence and analytical results indicate that grain
size and GB density constitute the primary distinguishing features
among current LDSs. Therefore, the difference in corrosion behavior can
be reasonably attributed to changes in the oxide film properties resulting
from grain size variation.
Previous studies[88–92] reported that GB segregation of alloying
elements such as Cr and V significantly influences the corrosion
resistance of the material. These studies suggest that elemental segre
gation at GBs may either promote the formation of stable passive films or
lead to precipitates that serve as pitting initiation sites, thereby affecting
corrosion performance. In contrast, the present study reveals a relatively
homogeneous elemental distribution without noticeable GB segregation.
The oxide film formation mechanism in this case appears to be pre
dominantly governed by the intrinsic structural characteristics of GBs,
which act as inherent surface defects of the crystal. Specifically, the
crystallographic misorientation between adjacent grains causes sub
stantial atomic disorder at HAGBs, which generates structural defects
that include lattice distortion, vacancy accumulation, and coordination
deficiencies[93,94]. These defects thermodynamically increase the
interfacial free energy at GBs to levels substantially higher than those in
grain interiors, thereby enhancing their susceptibility to anodic disso
lution in electrochemical systems[95–98]. From a kinetic perspective,
the weaker binding energy of boundary atoms decreases the activation
energy required for metal ion dissolution from the crystal lattice. The
structural disorder coupled with vacancy accumulation creates
short-circuit diffusion pathways, which significantly promote the
dissolution activity of GBs in corrosive environments[99–102]. When
selective anodic dissolution initiates at GB, the local metal ion concen
tration rises sharply while the interfacial
\mathtt { p H }
value declines. This acidi
fication effect narrows the thermodynamic passive region and lowers
the critical energy barrier for oxide film nucleation[100,103]. Concur
rently, GBs serve as continuous permeation networks that facilitate both
the inward migration of water molecules and the outward diffusion of
metal cations. The synergistic interaction of these processes within GB
defect regions enables rapid nucleation and growth of oxide films[104,
105]. Consequently, even without elemental segregation, GBs govern
both the initial dissolution behavior and subsequent oxide film forma
tion due to their higher interfacial free energy and lower dissolution
barriers.
